syllabus.clause: spotting flow, matching, 2-SAT, shortest path, interval scheduling or DP on a DAG inside a word problem

at.step: Flow and cut: something moves from sources to sinks through capacity-limited links. The reviewer assignment, built as a flow network, places all eight reviews — confirmed by the flow algorithm and by an independent brute-force search over every valid assignment. The near-miss: a flow that must be routed as whole, indivisible units along single paths is a much harder problem.

Matching: pair items from two groups, each used at most once. The structural fact is that the graph is bipartite — every edge crosses from one side to the other. Two different algorithms, the Kuhn augmenting-path method and the flow-based one, agree on three pairs for the identical instance. The near-miss: pairing within a single group, with an odd cycle, is not bipartite at all, confirmed directly by checking for one.

Two-SAT: a set of yes-or-no choices with constraints that each involve at most two of them. Built as an implication graph and solved by strongly connected components — satisfiable exactly when no variable and its negation land in the same component, confirmed against brute-force truth tables on both a satisfiable and an unsatisfiable instance. The near-miss is the sharpest in the chapter: the identical shape with three choices per constraint is three-SAT, NP-complete.

Interval scheduling: activities with start and end times competing for one resource. Sorting by finish time and greedily taking what still fits finds four non-overlapping intervals, matching an exhaustive brute-force search exactly. The near-miss: the identical story with several resource types, or with setup time between jobs, is general scheduling and typically NP-hard.

DP on a DAG: a decision sequence where each step depends only on earlier ones and nothing repeats. Relaxing a small dependency graph in topological order finds the longest path exactly, matching a full enumeration of every path through it. The near-miss: the identical relaxation breaks the moment the dependency graph has a cycle, and a longest path in a graph with cycles is the Hamiltonian-cycle family of problems, NP-hard.
